sentences.text: Bagaceratops was one of the smallest ceratopsians, reaching lengths of 1 to 1.5 meters and weighing between 22.7 and 45 kilograms.
This dinosaur belonged to the group Ceratopsia, which included herbivorous dinosaurs with parrot-like beaks.
Unlike its close relative Protoceratops, Bagaceratops lacked frontal horns and possessed only a small prominence on the snout.
The skull featured fused nasal bones and an accessory antorbital fenestra in the maxilla, while the animal lacked premaxillary teeth.
It had a smaller, triangular tail compared to its relatives.
Evidence of invertebrate scavengers on the joints of a Bagaceratops skeleton was analyzed in 2010 and 2011.
The species is known from five complete skulls and twenty partials showing various life stages, making its growth cycle well understood.
The first fossils were discovered in the Gobi Desert during the 1970s by a joint Polish-Mongolian expedition.
The genus Bagaceratops was named in 1975 by Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska for the species Bagaceratops rozhdestvenskyi.
The name means "small-horned face", derived from Mongolian and Greek words.
An articulated and nearly complete skeleton was collected in 1993 from the Barun Goyot Formation.
Fossils have been found in the Barun Goyot and Bayan Mandahu Formations, with one specimen suggesting the animal may also have lived in the Djadochta Formation.
The animal was initially named Protoceratops kozlowskii, later renamed Breviceratops kozlowskii by Kurzanov in 1990, and is now considered Bagaceratops.
Like all ceratopsians, Bagaceratops was a herbivore that likely ate dominant plants of its time such as ferns, cycads, and conifers.
A new family named Bagaceratopsidae has been proposed to include Bagaceratops.

Bagaceratops lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 71 million years ago, though the time range is debated from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
It lived in alluvial plain, lacustrine, and aeolian environments under relatively arid to semiarid climates.
The Bayan Mandahu Formation, which yielded Magnirostris (now a synonym of Bagaceratops), is considered Late Cretaceous, roughly Campanian.
Some researchers consider Breviceratops a distinct genus separate from Bagaceratops and Protoceratops due to its mix of primitive and advanced traits.
It is debated whether Bagaceratops should be placed in its own family, Bagaceratopsidae, or remain within Protoceratopsidae.
